stories.headline: Flooding strands about 100 people in Archuleta County as river crests
stories.summary:
About 100 people were cut off by washed-out roads in Archuleta County after flooding pushed the river to a peak of more than a dozen feet early Friday, Sheriff Mike Le Roux said. The river crested around 5:30 a.m., with most of the high water arriving in the dark. Le Roux said the forecast called for significantly more water than officials had expected.

Crews worked to reach a vehicle stranded in the river with two adults and three pets, and a National Guard Black Hawk with hoist capability was expected to help. Le Roux said he was not aware of any deaths or significant injuries. Many of the stranded residents live in areas that were not under an evacuation order or warning, and he described them as safe but landlocked.

Le Roux said roads were cut through at culverts where water flowed for 12 to 16 hours, damaging state, county and private infrastructure. He said this flood brought more surface runoff and localized flooding than last year's, which was itself unprecedented. The river could see another short spike Saturday, though not at the same peak.

The Colorado Division of Fire Prevention and Control launched its Multi-Mission Aircraft and requested two helicopters, along with about 10 incident management personnel and two engines with crews. Le Roux said recovery is expected to be long and that he is working with state emergency management and the governor's office.

stories.headline: Colorado State Patrol investigates 10 crashes along stretch of I-25 in Larimer County
stories.summary:
A string of crashes involving stopped traffic, rear-end collisions and two hit-and-runs disrupted southbound Interstate 25 in northern Colorado on Friday morning, according to Colorado State Patrol. The agency said it was investigating a high volume of crashes on a single stretch of the highway in Larimer County.

Troopers documented 10 separate crashes across the corridor. The collisions affected southbound travel during the morning commute and prompted an extended investigation.

The crashes are a reminder of the hazards of stop-and-go traffic on the Front Range's main north-south corridor. Drivers who use the route between northern Colorado and the Denver metro area were affected by the disruptions.

stories.headline: Bear attacks man outside his Clear Creek County home
stories.summary:
A bear attacked a man outside his home in Clear Creek County early Thursday after he found it near trash cans and tried to scare it off, Colorado Parks and Wildlife officials said. The attack happened about 1 a.m. outside a home on Castlewood Drive. The homeowner heard noises on the deck and came upon the bear.

The man yelled to drive the bear away, but it charged him multiple times and left only after he kicked it in self-defense. He sought medical treatment, though officials did not say how badly he was hurt. Wildlife officers responded but could not find the bear, and they will keep searching for bear activity.

Colorado has had an unprecedented number of bear encounters in 2026 as a severe drought has deprived bears of natural food sources while they try to bulk up for winter hibernation. Officials urged residents to secure food, garbage and recycling outdoors, remove bird feeders when bears are active, avoid leaving pet food outside, and store grills securely.

stories.headline: Nuggets rally from 23 down to beat Pelicans 141-135 in overtime in home opener
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets erased a 23-point deficit to beat the New Orleans Pelicans 141-135 in overtime Saturday in their home opener at Ball Arena. Denver trailed by 19 in the fourth quarter and 126-119 with 1:19 left before Jamal Murray's two free throws tied the game at 126 and forced overtime. It was only the sixth time in franchise history Denver has won after trailing by 22 or more in the second half.

Murray scored 42 points with eight three-pointers. Nikola Jokic had 35 points, 15 rebounds and 10 assists, scoring eight in overtime, and his 222nd triple-double set the NBA record for regular-season and postseason triple-doubles. Rookie Trevon Brazile added 17 points and two blocks, and the crowd chanted "MVP" for him.

Denver played without Cameron Johnson, who missed the game with an ankle injury, and coach David Adelman chose Brazile over newcomer DeMar DeRozan in the closing rotation. Adelman called the first half "horrendous" but said he liked the fight back. The Pelicans fell to 0-3.

stories.headline: Jokic says Nuggets fans who booed in home opener are 'not welcome anymore'
stories.summary:
Nikola Jokic criticized fans who booed the Nuggets during Saturday's home opener, which Denver won 141-135 in overtime over the New Orleans Pelicans. Fans booed after the Nuggets fell behind 45-26 early in the second quarter and trailed 73-57 at halftime.

"I think those fans who booed us, they don't need to come anymore," Jokic said. "If they ask me, they are not welcome anymore." He added that anyone who follows the team knows it never quits, but said Nuggets fans should support the team.

Coach David Adelman called the first-half effort dismal and horrendous. Aaron Gordon said the team needs to stop starting games so poorly, warning it cannot play lackadaisically for three quarters against contenders and expect to be let back in.

stories.headline: Renck: Broncos should trade for Colts running back Jonathan Taylor
stories.summary:
Denver Post columnist Troy Renck argues the Broncos should trade for Indianapolis running back Jonathan Taylor as the team's run game struggles six weeks into the season. Denver is 4-2 and hosts the Arizona Cardinals on Sunday.

J.K. Dobbins, re-signed to a two-year, $16 million deal after the Broncos balked at Travis Etienne's demand of four years and $47 million, has 270 yards on 81 carries, a career-low 3.3 yards per attempt. He has also dealt with a hamstring issue. Renck notes Bo Nix is in a slump and the team has scored just 11 offensive touchdowns.

Taylor has rushed for 492 yards, sixth in the NFL, and is tied for the league lead with seven touchdowns on a Colts team without a general manager. Renck contrasts Denver with Kansas City, whose offense has been transformed by Kenneth Walker III and who the Broncos face next week in a game he calls a must-win for the AFC West.

stories.headline: Bavarian Guild's inaugural Oktoberfest brings Munich-style celebration to National Western Center
stories.summary:
The Bavarian Guild of Colorado and Wyoming hosted a new Oktoberfest celebration at the National Western Center in Denver. Founder and CEO Chadwick Williams said the event stands apart for its authenticity, family-friendly atmosphere and multicultural focus. "It's not beer and brats," he said, describing it as a chance to sit across from strangers and build community.

Williams said the guild, less than a year old, brokered an economic partnership between Denver and Munich, signed by Mayor Mike Johnston and Munich Mayor Dominik Krause. He called it the first economic partnership between Denver and any part of Germany.

The festival offered Bavarian food, Hofbräu Munich beer, live music and dancing, free entry and a 110-foot Ferris wheel. Attendees said it was smaller than Munich's festival but lively, though some wanted the site built out more. Saturday marked the second weekend of events.

topStory.headline: Ramaswamy Ad Featuring Acton's Estranged Mother Draws Bipartisan Criticism as Records Detail Family's Troubled Past
topStory.summary:
An attack advertisement from Republican Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy targeting Democratic opponent Amy Acton has drawn criticism, including from within his own party, less than two weeks before the November 3 midterm elections. The ad, which began circulating online on Monday, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who calls her daughter a liar, disputes her account of childhood homelessness and living in a tent, and suggests she has a mental illness. Ramaswamy's campaign confirmed on Tuesday that it was behind the ad and announced plans to spend $4 million promoting it. Ramaswamy has refused to withdraw it despite calls from senior Republicans to do so.

The ad does not mention that Acton and her mother have been estranged since 1978, when Acton, then 12, was removed from her mother's custody after her stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her. According to court records obtained by Signal Ohio, he pleaded not guilty but failed to appear in court and was never tried. Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death. Court records and contemporaneous news reports support key elements of Acton's account, and FactCheck.org found records linking the stepfather to the campground where Acton said the family lived in a tent, contradicting Arthur's claim that the family never lived there.

Public records and newspaper clippings reviewed by NBC News and court records obtained by NewsNation also show a history of financial and legal trouble for Donna Arthur. A Clearfield County, Pennsylvania, indictment charged her with theft by deception and bad checks related to $2,555 in purchases at a September 1995 auction; she pleaded guilty in 1996 and received a maximum sentence of 24 months in confinement. She pleaded guilty to another series of similar charges in 2005. In 2021, she faced animal neglect charges alleging she kept cats and kittens in a locked vehicle with an internal temperature of 120 degrees Fahrenheit; at least one resulting conviction was later vacated on appeal for denial of counsel. NewsNation said it had reached out to Arthur for comment.

Acton's campaign responded Tuesday with a statement recounting her childhood and a counter-ad featuring her brother, Phil Stearns, who said, "I received a lot of abuse, but Amy always got the worst of it. She continued to receive that abuse because she knew she had to protect me." David Niven, a political science professor at the University of Cincinnati, told Al Jazeera that campaigns have used relatives against candidates before, but not in such a deeply personal way, calling the "degree of just personal destruction" unprecedented.

President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended Ramaswamy, and Trump described the ad on Thursday as "very powerful" and said he had encouraged Ramaswamy to continue. The dispute has raised broader questions about the limits of personal attacks in campaigns and how voters will respond in the closing days of the Ohio governor's race. With a $4 million ad buy planned, the spot is expected to remain a prominent feature of the contest through Election Day.
